PROPOSED AMENDMENTS TO
ARTICLES II AND V
First—That Section 15 of Article II thereof is amended
to read:
SEC. 15. (a) An election to determine whether to
recall an officer and, if appropriate, to elect a successor
shall be called by the Governor and held not less than
60 days nor more than 80 days from the date of
certification of sufficient signatures.
(b) A recall election may be conducted within 180 days
from the date of certification of sufficient signatures in
order that the election may be consolidated with the
next regularly scheduled election occurring wholly or
partially within the same jurisdiction in which the recall
election is held, if the number of voters eligible to vote
at that next regularly scheduled election equal at least
50 percent of all the voters eligible to vote at the recall
election.
(c) If the majority vote on the question is to recall, the
officer is removed and, if there is a candidate, the
candidate who receives a plurality is the successor. The
officer may not be a candidate, nor shall there be any
candidacy for an office filled pursuant to subdivision (d)
of Section 16 of Article VI. and the office shall be
vacant. The vacancy shall be filled in accordance with
this Constitution and statute, provided that the officer
who was the subject of the recall election shall not be
appointed to fill the vacancy in that office.

amended to read:
SEC. 17. If recall of the Governor or Secretary of
State is initiated, the recall duties of that office shall be
performed by the Lieutenant Governor Secretary of

Governor and Secretary of State are initiated at the
same time, the recall duties of both offices shall be
performed by the Controller.
Third—That Section 10 of Article V thereof is amended

SEC. 10. (a) The Lieutenant Governor shall become
Governor when a vacancy occurs in the office of
Governor.

recall, the Lieutenant Governor shall become Governor
for the remainder of the unexpired term. If the Governor

nomination period for the next statewide election during

shall be consolidated with the statewide primary

shall become Governor for the remainder of the

the votes, the top two vote-getters shall compete in a
special election consolidated with the subsequent
statewide general election, and the winner of that
election shall become Governor for the remainder of the
unexpired term.
(c) The Lieutenant Governor shall act as Governor
during the impeachment, absence from the State, or
other temporary disability of the Governor or of a

(d) The Legislature shall provide an order of
precedence after the Lieutenant Governor for
succession to the office of Governor and for the
temporary exercise of the Governor’s functions.
(e) The Supreme Court has exclusive jurisdiction to
determine all questions arising under this section.
(f) Standing to raise questions of vacancy or temporary
disability is vested exclusively in a body provided by
statute.

Also let me check CalMatters coverage, which usually has a good "explain" piece and a "what would Prop 5 do" analysis. Let me also check the actual text of the law for details on the recalled-official-running-again provision.

Key facts so far:
- Prop 5 (Nov 2026): removes the second question (who replaces the recalled official) from recall ballots for state officials.
- For Governor: LG becomes Governor; if recall happens early in term (before nomination period for next statewide election during first two years), voters elect a new Governor at the next statewide election; otherwise LG serves out the term.
- Other statewide offices: Governor appoints replacement.
- Legislative seats: special election.
- Removes the current constitutional ban on recalled officials running to fill their own vacancy (Prop 5 allows recalled officials to run in the special election to replace themselves).
- Fiscal effect: unknown; could be savings or costs of millions per election.
- Support: League of Women Voters, Common Cause CA, CA Democratic Party, CA Labor Federation, former FPPC chair Dan Schnur, Secretary of State (placed on ballot by Legislature — actually the measure was SCA 1 / SCA 2?), authored by Josh Newman.
- Opposition: Republicans (Senate Minority Leader Brian Jones, Assemblymember Joe Patterson), Election Integrity Project California.
- PPIC poll: 59% likely voters say they'd vote against, 35% in favor.
- Endorsements: LA Times/Skelton: Yes. SF Chronicle: No (due to the provision allowing recalled officials to run in replacement election — "glaring flaw" even the author couldn't explain). Mercury News/East Bay Times/Santa Cruz Sentinel (BANG): No. San Diego U-T: No. Press Enterprise/SCNG: No. Sacramento Bee: need to check.

The question asks me to decide whether it's better to vote yes or no and answer with only "yes" or "no".

Let me think about the merits:

Arguments FOR Prop 5 (Yes):
1. The current two-question setup is undemocratic: a replacement can win with a tiny plurality (e.g., in 2021, Larry Elder could have won with ~28% support even if a majority opposed the recall... wait, actually if the recall failed, the replacement votes wouldn't matter. The concern is that if the recall succeeded with say 51-52%, the replacement would win with far less than a majority of total voters). In 2003, Schwarzenegger won with ~48.6% in a 135-candidate field. This is a real flaw.
2. It creates perverse incentives for partisan gamesmanship — a well-funded minority can trigger a recall (12% of last election's turnout for statewide) and potentially install someone with a small plurality.
3. It reduces cost/clutter: no need for a 46-135 candidate replacement list.
4. The replacement process would match the standard vacancy process — which most states use. Only 6-7 other states use the two-question format. Most recall states fill vacancies by succession or appointment.
5. Continuity: LG (separately elected, statewide) becomes governor — this is the same as if the governor died or resigned. It's the constitutional line of succession.
6. Good government groups (LWV, Common Cause) support it.

Arguments AGAINST (No):
1. Takes power away from voters: voters would no longer choose the replacement; instead the Governor appoints (for statewide offices other than governor) or a special election happens later.
2. For a gubernatorial recall, the LG — likely an ally of the recalled governor — would take over, arguably defying the will of the voters who just recalled the governor. Opponents call this a way for the party in power to neutralize recalls.
3. Costs: special elections for legislative seats could cost millions, and seats sit vacant for months.
4. The "bizarre flaw": it lifts the current constitutional ban on recalled officials running in the replacement election — meaning an official just recalled could run to regain their own seat. The SF Chronicle found this egregious; even the author couldn't explain it.
5. Motivation is questionable — authored by a former senator (Josh Newman) who was recalled in 2018 after voting for a gas tax increase. Critics see it as sour grapes/"Newman's Revenge" aimed at weakening a tool used against incumbents.
6. It could reduce accountability: the threat of recall is diminished if the successor is chosen by appointment rather than voters... though the recall itself remains available.
7. The problem is rare: only 11 state recalls since 1913, 6 successful. Fixing a "non-broken" system.
8. PPIC poll shows voters oppose it 59-35.

Hmm. The question: "Is it better to vote yes or no on this prop?" I need to weigh the arguments.

Let me think about what's genuinely better policy:

The core reform — eliminating the two-question ballot — addresses a genuine democratic defect: in a recall of the governor, a candidate could win office with, say, 25-30% of the vote while the governor is removed with just over 50%. That's a real problem. But note the counter-argument: in 2003, Schwarzenegger won 48.58% of the replacement vote, more votes than votes to recall Davis... Actually, Schwarzenegger got 4.2 million replacement votes vs 4.7 million "yes on recall" — and Bustamante got 2.9 million. The "yes on recall" total (4.7M) was more than Schwarzenegger's votes. Some argue the 2003 system worked fine.

However, there are deeper problems with Prop 5:
1. The provision allowing recalled officials to run in the replacement special election. Currently, the California Constitution (Art. II, Sec. 15... actually Government Code 11320?) — wait, the SF Chronicle says it overturns a ban in the California Constitution. Let me verify: California Constitution Article II, Section 15: "An election to determine whether to recall an officer and, if appropriate, to elect a successor shall be called..." Hmm, the ban on recalled officials running as successor: Elections Code section 11382 prohibits a recalled officer from being a candidate for successor. The Chronicle cites the Constitution — actually the California Constitution Art. II Sec. 17(c) says "If the majority vote on the question is to recall, the officer is removed..." Hmm. Let me check the actual text.

Actually, the state constitution doesn't explicitly ban it — Government Code §11381 or Elections Code §11382 says: "A recalled officer is not eligible to be a candidate" — wait let me check. The Elections Code: §11382: "A recalled officer shall not be a candidate for the office..." Hmm. The Chronicle said "overturning a ban in the California Constitution" — let me check the text of Prop 5. Prop 5 is a constitutional amendment, so it can change constitutional provisions. If the ban is in statute, a constitutional amendment wouldn't need to overturn it, but the amendment could implicitly supersede.

Let me look at the actual text. Also, there's a subtlety: why allow the recalled official to run in the special election? The rationale given by supporters: this makes recall more like a normal process, and lets voters decide. Hmm, actually there's a genuine argument: under current law, a recalled official is banned from being on the successor list — but Prop 5 proponents argue that in a special election scenario, the recalled official should be allowed to make their case to voters (this avoids the "one bad vote (e.g., gas tax) and you're permanently out" problem). But critics say it lets a well-funded incumbent (who can raise unlimited funds under recall rules) win back their seat.

2. The gubernatorial succession issue: if a governor is recalled late in term, the LG serves out the rest of the term. The LG is usually of the same party as the governor. Under the current system, voters choose the replacement. So a recall election under Prop 5 essentially only removes the person, not the administration. Opponents argue this means recalls become pointless — you'd just get the LG. But wait — is that bad? If the voters want to remove the governor for misconduct, they can still remove them; the LG is a separately elected statewide official. This is how vacancy succession works in most contexts and in most states. In most other recall states, the LG or another successor takes over. Also, a "yes" recall under Prop 5 still expresses voter will.

But a deeper problem: a partisan minority could still trigger a recall, and the effect would just be to swap Governor → LG of the same party — pointless churn costing $200M. But the current system has its own pathologies.

3. For legislative recalls, the seat sits vacant until a special election (months), leaving the district unrepresented — and the recalled official can run again in that special election! That's a weird outcome: voters recall someone, then they might win the seat back months later with the same or even less support (special election turnout is low). Meanwhile the district is unrepresented. This seems to weaken the recall's meaning: it effectively becomes a "re-do" election where the incumbent has huge fundraising advantages.

Actually wait — that's a good point. Under Prop 5, a legislative recall becomes: (a) recall vote removes them, (b) special election months later, (c) they can run again. So the recall's practical effect is to force a re-election, not removal. Under the current system, the recall definitively removes them and installs the voters' chosen replacement. Under Prop 5, the recall might not even result in removal in substance — the same person could return. This significantly weakens the recall as an accountability tool. That's the U-T's argument ("power play") and the Chronicle's argument (the "glaring flaw").

Hmm, so the policy trade-off:
- Yes: fixes the "replacement with 25% plurality" problem, aligns with most states, reduces ballot clutter and potential cost, endorsed by good-government groups (LWV, Common Cause).
- No: preserves voter choice of replacement, avoids empowering governors to appoint replacements and the LG to inherit the office without any election, avoids leaving seats vacant, avoids the weird provision letting recalled officials run to replace themselves, and avoids a measure that appears primarily designed to protect incumbents (authored by someone who was recalled).

The PPIC poll shows 59% of likely voters oppose. Many editorial boards (Mercury News/East Bay Times, SF Chronicle, San Diego U-T, Press Enterprise, SCNG papers) recommend No. LA Times's George Skelton recommends Yes. CalMatters? Let me check. Also the Sacramento Bee — let me check its editorial.

Let me also check the LA Times editorial board (not Skelton's column, which is a personal column). Hmm, the LA Times seems to have endorsed... Let me check. The LA Times typically does ballot measure endorsements. In the search result, I see a Skelton newsletter recommending Yes. Let me search for "Los Angeles Times editorial board Proposition 5 endorsement recall."

Also let me consider the history: SCA 1 (Newman) was passed by the Legislature in 2024. It also removes the requirement... Another element: the measure removes the ban on recalled officials running for their old seat. Let me verify by reading the text of the proposed law.

Let me also think about who's behind it: The California Democratic Party, Labor Federation. The measure is largely seen as a Democratic establishment effort to prevent a repeat of 2003 (when Schwarzenegger, a Republican, won the recall replacement race in a blue state). Republicans oppose. Good government groups split: LWV and Common Cause support; Election Integrity Project opposes (that group is more conservative).

Let me weigh the strongest considerations:

Real flaws in current system:
- Plurality winner problem (genuine but historically, 2003 winner had 48.6%; 2021 had 46 candidates where the leading replacement was polling around 30-38% — yes, that's a genuine problem).
- Confusing two-question ballot.
- Encourages recall attempts as "redo" elections by well-funded minorities.

Real flaws in Prop 5:
- Removes voter choice of replacement (a real power shift toward the governor and LG — political insiders).
- Vacancy periods for legislative seats; extra special elections cost millions.
- The provision allowing recalled officials to run in their own replacement election — a significant flaw that even the author can't explain, and it makes recall substantively weaker (they can come back).
- Perceived incumbent-protection motivation.

Now, which matters more? The 2021 Newsom recall is the key case study: it failed, Newsom stayed. Under Prop 5, a future Newsom-like recall that succeeded would install the LG (Kounalakis, a Democrat) — so the recall's effect on governance would be nil in practice for a governor recall late in term. That is arguably the point: recall of a governor becomes about removing the individual, and the successor is the separately elected LG. Is that bad? Compare with 2003: Davis removed, Schwarzenegger (R) elected with 48.6% in a wave of dissatisfaction with Davis. Under Prop 5, Davis would have been replaced by Cruz Bustamante (the LG, a Democrat). The 2003 recall reflected deep voter dissatisfaction with Davis's performance and the state's direction — voters wanted a change in direction. Under Prop 5, that desire would have been thwarted until the next scheduled election (March 2004 primary? Davis was recalled Oct 2003; the 2004 election... the recall was in the first year of Davis's second term, so under Prop 5, would voters elect a new governor at the March 2004 primary? The nomination period for the next statewide election... the recall happened in October 2003; the next statewide election was March 2004 primary, whose nomination period would have closed around... December 2003/January 2004. If the recall occurred before the close of the nomination period, the LG serves until the next statewide election (March 2004 primary) where voters elect a new governor. Hmm, that could mean a very quick new gubernatorial election in March 2004.)

Wait, let me re-read the provision: "If the Governor is recalled before the close of the nomination period for the next statewide election during the first two years of the term, Proposition 5 says that the Lieutenant Governor serves as Governor until voters elect a new Governor at a future statewide election." So for 2003: recall Oct 7, 2003 (first year of Davis's 2nd term). Next statewide election: March 2, 2004 primary. Nomination period for that closed around... December 5, 2003? Hmm, actually if the recall occurred before the close of the nomination period, then the LG serves "until voters elect a new Governor at a future statewide election" — so Bustamante would serve until the March 2004 election, where a new governor would be elected. But wait — would candidates for governor have been able to file for the March 2004 ballot? The nomination period would already be underway/closed... This gets complicated. Actually the LA Times commentary said: "If so, a special election would be held on the same date as the next primary and a candidate receiving a majority of votes would serve out the governor's term." So the gubernatorial vacancy election would be held on the next primary date (March 2004 in the 2003 example), with a majority requirement and top-two runoff if needed.

So in the 2003 scenario: Davis recalled, Bustamante serves ~5 months, then a March 2004 gubernatorial election decides who serves out the term. That's not so bad actually — voters get to choose the new governor in a regular-ish election within months, and the winner needs a majority (with runoff). That's much more majoritarian than the 2003 plurality scramble.

For 2021 Newsom scenario: The recall was Sept 14, 2021 — Newsom's first term began Jan 2019, so Sept 2021 was in the third year of his first term. "During the first two years of the term" — Sept 2021 is in year 3. Hmm, so if the recall had succeeded in 2021, the LG (Kounalakis) would have served out the rest of the term through Jan 2023. Then the regularly scheduled 2022 election would choose the next governor. So the incumbent party keeps the governorship for ~1.3 years, then a regular election. Voters still voted in Nov 2022 anyway. The "harm" is that voters' replacement choice (Elder, at ~24-28% in polls) is overridden... but honestly, is it worse for the LG to hold office until the next scheduled election than for someone with 25% support to win? Debatable — the LG is a statewide-elected official too (Kounalakis won statewide in 2018 with more votes than Newsom? No, she won her own race).

For non-governor statewide offices: the Governor appoints the replacement — this is the existing vacancy process for e.g. if the AG resigns. The appointed person serves until the next election. Fine, but note: a recall of, say, a Republican insurance commissioner in a Democratic administration would result in a Democrat being appointed to replace them — the recall could literally flip the office to the other party via gubernatorial appointment. Under current rules, voters choose the replacement, so a recalled R official would likely be replaced by another R (or whoever voters pick). Under Prop 5, the recall vote becomes: remove the official AND effectively hand the office to the Governor's party. That's a perverse incentive for the party controlling the governorship to weaponize recalls of the opposing party's statewide officeholders! Interesting — both parties could weaponize it, but the party with the governorship has the edge. This is a genuine new loophole: recall the other party's AG/SoS/Controller, and your party's governor appoints a member of your own party. That's a real flaw that commentators have noted? Let me think... Actually, under Prop 5, a recall of a constitutional officer would be followed by gubernatorial appointment. So recalls become a partisan tool for the governor's party to flip seats. Hmm, that could actually increase the incentive for partisan recalls, not decrease it! (Though the recall threshold is 12% of the last election's votes — achievable with money.)

Wait, but that's the same as the existing vacancy process — if an official dies/resigns, the governor appoints. The difference: a recall is a forced vacancy. So yes, Prop 5 creates the possibility of using recall to flip partisan control of offices via appointment. That's a strong argument against, IMO. For example: California has a Republican... hmm, currently all statewide offices are held by Democrats (as of 2026, after the 2022 election, all statewide offices are D). Not very relevant in current CA. But the mechanics matter long-term.

For legislative seats: special election, and the recalled member can run. Under the current rules, the replacement is chosen on the same ballot. Under Prop 5: months of vacancy, millions in special election costs, and the recalled official can win the seat back. This weakens the recall and costs more.

So Prop 5's core fix (majoritarian succession) comes bundled with: gubernatorial appointment power over recalled constitutional officers, vacancy gaps, extra costs, and the recalled-official-can-run-again provision.

The Chronicle's view: "We agree that the second question is problematic and we might support its removal in isolation. But Prop 5 contains a completely unnecessary provision that permits recalled officials to run in the very special election designed to replace them... reason enough for voters to reject this measure."

Current: "If recall of the Governor or Secretary of State is initiated, the recall duties of that office shall be performed by the Lieutenant Governor or Controller, respectively." Proposed: "If recall of the Governor or Lieutenant Governor is initiated, the recall duties of that office shall be performed by the Secretary of State or Controller, respectively. If recalls of the Governor and Lieutenant Governor are initiated at the same time, the recall duties of both offices shall be performed by the Controller."

That makes sense: currently, if the Governor's recall is initiated, the LG performs the Governor's recall duties (scheduling etc.) — which is a conflict since the LG is the likely successor candidate (they can run in the replacement race). Under Prop 5, since the LG just becomes governor, the SoS performs the Governor's recall duties; and if the LG's own recall is initiated, the Controller performs the LG's recall duties. That's a sensible conflict-of-interest fix.

So the actual mechanics:
- Recall ballot: single question.
- Governor recalled: LG becomes Governor. If recalled early in term (before close of nomination period for the next statewide election in the first two years), voters elect a replacement at the next statewide primary (majority + runoff at general). If later, LG serves the remainder.
- Other statewide officers recalled: vacancy filled per existing rules → Governor appoints (through the end of... typically the appointee serves until the next election — actually for constitutional officers, appointees serve the remainder? For vacancies in statewide offices, the Governor appoints; for some offices the appointee serves until the next election... In California, an appointed AG/SoS etc. serves the remainder of the term? Let me not get bogged down. Actually: Governor's appointment fills the vacancy; under Prop 128-era rules... For statewide constitutional offices, the appointee serves the balance of the term. E.g., Alex Padilla appointed to replace Kamala Harris as Senator served until the next election, but that's US Senate. For state constitutional offices — when Xavier Becerra resigned as AG, Becerra was replaced by Rob Bonta who served the remainder of the term (then won election). Yes, appointees to constitutional offices serve the remainder.
- Legislators recalled: special election (existing vacancy rules), and the recalled legislator can run in it.

Now, the analysis. Let me weigh:

The strongest pro argument: the plurality-winner successor problem. This is real. In 2021, Larry Elder led replacement polls with ~38% in some polls but the field was 46; he could have won with a quarter of the vote in a state of 22 million voters, while Newsom had won 2018 by 62-38. That's genuinely undemocratic. Good government groups (LWV, Common Cause) back the reform. Most states with recalls don't have same-day successor elections.

The strongest con arguments:
(a) The measure's motivation: authored by Josh Newman (recalled in 2018 after the gas tax vote) and placed on the ballot by legislative Democrats after the 2021 Newsom recall. It looks like incumbent/Democratic establishment protection. The "Newman's Revenge" narrative. However, on the merits, motivation doesn't determine whether the policy is good.
(b) The provision allowing recalled officials to run in the replacement special election. Confirmed in the text: the current "The officer may not be a candidate" line is deleted, and only an appointment ban is added. This is a genuine, unforced flaw. Effects: a recalled legislator can run in the special election to fill their own seat — months later, low turnout, and they keep unlimited recall-defense funds? (The Chronicle points out incumbents facing recall can raise unlimited contributions; using that war chest in the special election is a big advantage.) So the recall becomes a temporary suspension rather than removal. This severely undermines the recall's accountability function for legislators. And for the governor case in the first-two-years scenario, could the recalled Governor run in the special election to replace themselves? The text of Art. V Sec 10(b) doesn't prohibit it; Art. II Sec 15(c) as amended only prohibits *appointment* of the recalled officer to the vacancy. So a recalled governor could run in the special election to succeed themselves! That is bizarre: e.g., a governor recalled in year 1 could run in the primary-months-later to get the office back. Combined with the LG serving in the interim, the recall's meaning is diluted.
(c) Governor-appointment power for other statewide offices — a partisan flip mechanism.
(d) Cost/vacancy for legislative seats.
(e) Popular opposition: PPIC 59-35 against.

Counter-considerations for a Yes: the LWV/Common Cause/Schnur argument — recall's original purpose is removal, not installing a successor via 25% plurality; alignment with vacancy rules; majority-rule protection; the gubernatorial early-term special election with majority + runoff is a clean majoritarian process.

Hmm. Also note: the recalled-official-running-again provision has a defenders' rationale: it makes recalls less "one-strike-and-out" — e.g., Newman himself was recalled over a single gas-tax vote, then re-elected in 2020, showing voters actually wanted him. Letting the recalled official run in the special election lets voters make the final call. One could argue this is *more* democratic (the special election is a normal election with normal campaign finance limits, unlike the recall replacement free-for-all... wait, is the special election subject to normal contribution limits? Yes, special elections have normal limits. The unlimited fundraising applies to committees "controlled by an officeholder who is the subject of a recall" — Gov. Code 85315. Could that money be used in the special election? The Chronicle says state law prohibits using recall-defense money for other campaigns, but a recalled official in a special election... "is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received." OK.)

So how do I weigh this? The question asks for a recommendation: yes or no.

Consider the decision-relevant factors:

1. Frequency: recalls are rare (11 on ballot since 1913, 6 successful). The measure's practical effect is small either way. But constitutional rules matter for the big event (gubernatorial recall).

2. The central question: who should fill a vacancy created by recall — the voters simultaneously (plurality), or via standard vacancy rules (succession/appointment/special election)?

Most democratic theorists would say: the recall's purpose is removal; the successor should be chosen by a process that ensures majority support. The California two-question format is a genuine outlier (only ~6 states use it... actually NCSL: of the 19 states that allow recalls, some use same-day successor elections; CA's is unusual in its scale).

But Prop 5's implementation has real flaws: (a) the recalled official can run in the replacement election — undermines the whole point of recall; (b) gubernatorial appointment for other constitutional officers creates a partisan-flip incentive; (c) for governors recalled late in term, no voter choice at all (LG serves out term) — though arguably consistent with succession norms; (d) legislative vacancies/extra costs.

The Chronicle's position: might support removing the second question in isolation, but the flaw is reason to reject. Bay Area News Group, U-T, Press Enterprise: No. LA Times Skelton: Yes. CalMatters? Let me check. The Bee? Let me check quickly.

PPIC poll (Sept 2026): 59% no, 35% yes. That's voters, not a normative judgment.

Given the balance: editorial boards statewide mostly recommend No (SF Chronicle, Mercury News/East Bay Times, San Diego U-T, Press Enterprise, SCNG, Santa Cruz Sentinel, SGV Tribune). LA Times Skelton (personal column) Yes. I believe CalMatters doesn't endorse, but their "explain" piece might have a "who supports/opposes" breakdown.

The pros: LWV, Common Cause, CA Dem Party, Labor Federation, Dan Schnur.

The measure does fix a real problem, but introduces a worse one: allowing recalled officials to run to replace themselves turns recall into a do-over election with an incumbent advantage, and the appointment mechanism shifts power to the governor. Also, the strongest theoretical case for the two-question format is voter agency: Californians get to decide both removal and replacement directly — an abrupt but democratic system.

Actually, let me think again about the "recalled official can run" point more carefully, because it's decisive for many:

Current: recalled officer cannot be a candidate to succeed themselves (Cal. Const. Art. II Sec 15 — actually the current constitutional text says "The officer may not be a candidate" — wait, the current text in the strikeout shows: "If the majority vote on the question is to recall, the officer is removed and, if there is a candidate, the candidate who receives a plurality is the successor. The officer may not be a candidate, nor shall there be any candidacy for an office filled pursuant to subdivision (d) of Section 16 of Article VI." Hmm, "The officer may not be a candidate" — in the current constitution this means the recalled officer may not be a candidate for successor in the same recall election. And Prop 5 deletes this sentence and replaces with vacancy + no-appointment rule.

So yes: under Prop 5, a recalled official may run in the subsequent special election (for legislative seats or the early-term gubernatorial special election). Confirmed.

Is that bad? Consider: Newman was recalled in 2018 over the gas tax, then re-elected in 2020 to the same seat. His case shows that the voters of his district, given a normal election, chose him back. Under current rules, he was barred from the 2018 successor race. Under Prop 5, he could have run in the special election months later — and if his constituents still wanted him (like 2020), they could have him back quickly, saving the 2020 re-election. One could argue this is democratic — the recall question and the replacement question both get decided by voters.

But: the special election for a legislative recall would be scheduled by the Governor — the Governor (same party) controls timing, and could time it to advantage. The seat is vacant in the interim (unrepresented). And an incumbent who lost a 58-42 recall just months earlier could return. Also, opponents note the special election costs millions. And the majority that just voted to remove them would be overruled if the recalled official wins a plurality in a low-turnout special election. This makes recall substantively weaker — the threat of actual removal is reduced, which reduces the deterrent/accountability value of recall. Given recall is already a high bar (20% of prior turnout signatures for legislators), weakening it further protects incumbents.

On the other hand, the current system's weakness: a replacement can be installed with ~25% support, and the incumbent cannot be a candidate — meaning a slim majority can remove an official and install a successor with much less support. Both systems have pathologies. Which is worse?

Hmm. In 2003, the recall worked "as intended" per supporters: 55% removed Davis, Schwarzenegger won 48.6% of the replacement vote — arguably legitimate. In 2018, Newman's recall: 58-42 removal, Chang won the replacement. Turnout in recalls tends to be decent. The "28% Elder" scenario didn't happen because the recall failed. The plurality problem is real but has never actually produced a tiny-plurality governor.

Meanwhile, Prop 5's changes are prospective and untested. Key risks:
- Governor recall in year 3-4: LG (often the governor's political ally/ticketmate) takes over with zero additional voter input — the recall has no effect on policy direction. A well-funded minority (12% signatures) can force a $200M election and remove an individual, but nothing changes. This could actually make recalls *more* tempting for pure harassment (cost and chaos, no governance change), or less tempting (no partisan gain). Hmm, if there's no partisan gain, the incentive for partisan recalls goes DOWN — which is the proponents' argument. But it also means recall becomes purely punitive — removing a person while handing office to their lieutenant. Is that "restoring the recall to its original purpose" or neutering it?

The original purpose (1911 Progressive era): remove corrupt/unresponsive officials. Under Prop 5, removing a corrupt governor still removes them — the LG takes over — accountability achieved. Under current rules, the replacement is chosen by voters. The 1911 framers allowed the replacement election... The pro argument says "framers intended to safeguard voters against corrupt officials, not to provide a weapon for political operators."

Honestly, both sides have real arguments. Let me look at CalMatters and the LA Times editorial board's stance, plus maybe the Bee's editorial, then decide.

Also let me reconsider: the user just wants a yes/no recommendation. Given:
- The measure is opposed by a broad range of editorial boards across the state (left, center, right: SF Chronicle — center-left — No; Mercury News/East Bay Times No; SD U-T (right-leaning board) No; Press Enterprise (right) No; LA Times — let me check).
- PPIC: voters oppose 59-35.
- Good-government groups split: LWV/Common Cause yes, but others no.
- The measure contains the acknowledged flaw (recalled officials can run to replace themselves) that even its author couldn't justify.
- It shifts replacement power from voters to the Governor (appointments) and to the LG (succession).
- It creates partisan-flip incentives for constitutional officer recalls.
- Legislative recalls: vacancy + extra cost + weakened removal.

Versus:
- The genuine plurality-winner problem in the current system.
- Alignment with most states and with standard vacancy rules.
- Majority-rule: gubernatorial early-term replacement via majority special election.

I'm leaning "No" — the measure's flaws (the do-over provision, the appointment/succession power grab from voters, and the incumbent-protection motivation) outweigh the genuine but fixable problem of plurality successors. Also notably: California's recall has worked for a century; only 11 state recalls have qualified; the two-question format's pathologies have been rare; and this particular reform package is sloppy (the author himself couldn't explain a key provision). The Chronicle's reasoning — "we might support removal of the second question in isolation, but this flaw is reason enough to reject" — is a sound, centrist position.

But wait — let me double-check the LA Times editorial board. If the LA Times also endorsed Yes, the split is more balanced. Let me also check CalMatters and the Sacramento Bee. And maybe an academic (e.g., UC) analysis. Let me do a couple more searches.

Actually, let me also consider the counterfactual: if Prop 5 fails, the current system stays — including the possibility that in a future gubernatorial recall, someone wins with 25-30% of the vote. Is that a risk worth tolerating? The system has produced: 2003 (48.6% winner — fine), 2018 legislative recalls (Chang won replacement with plurality in a large field? She got ~50%+? Not sure). It's a live flaw. But Prop 5's alternative — LG succession or gubernatorial appointment — guarantees the replacement has NO fresh voter mandate at all (in the late-term gubernatorial case and the constitutional officer case), or a delayed majority-based mandate (early-term gubernatorial case; legislative case). Hmm, in the legislative case, the special election would use the normal top-two/majority process — actually legislative special elections in CA require a majority or top-two runoff. That's majoritarian. And the gubernatorial early-term special election requires a majority. So in 3 of 4 scenarios, Prop 5 actually produces majority-supported successors, better than plurality. The exception is late-term gubernatorial recall (LG serves remainder) and constitutional officers (gubernatorial appointment).

Eh. Honestly, this is a close call, and reasonable people disagree. The task: "Do extensive research... Answer with only yes or no." I need to commit.

Let me consider the meta-arguments:

For a "Yes" recommendation:
- LWV and Common Cause — nonpartisan good-government orgs with long histories — support. Dan Schnur (former FPPC chair, respected reformer) supports.
- Fixes a genuine democratic defect (plurality succession).
- Harmonizes recall with existing vacancy rules — simple, coherent.
- Reduces recall gamesmanship incentive (no partisan payoff for triggering recalls).

- Empowers governors to appoint replacements for recalled constitutional officers — creates partisan-flip incentives.
- Late-term gubernatorial recall: LG of the same party serves out the term; recall becomes functionally meaningless in governance terms.

- Motivation: incumbent protection after 2018 Newman recall and 2021 Newsom scare.
- Broad editorial opposition across the spectrum; PPIC shows strong voter opposition.
- The problem is rare; a better-designed reform could be adopted later.

Hmm, one more consideration: the "fix isn't dire" argument — 11 recalls qualified since 1913. The cost of a flawed reform outweighs the rare benefit. The Chronicle: "The problem isn't so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5's glaring flaw."

I think "No" is the better recommendation. The measure bundles a genuinely good idea (removing the plurality-successor question) with genuinely bad mechanics (allowing recalled officials to run to replace themselves; gubernatorial appointment power; late-term gubernatorial succession with no voter input; legislative vacancies and costs). On balance, the package reduces voter power and weakens accountability more than it improves majoritarian process. That makes sense: currently, if the Governor's recall is initiated, the LG performs the Governor's recall duties (scheduling etc.) — which is a conflict since the LG is the likely successor candidate (they can run in the replacement race). Under Prop 5, since the LG just becomes governor, the SoS performs the Governor's recall duties; and if the LG's own recall is initiated, the Controller performs the LG's recall duties. That's a sensible conflict-of-interest fix.

So the actual mechanics:
- Recall ballot: single question.
- Governor recalled: LG becomes Governor. If recalled early in term (before close of nomination period for the next statewide election in the first two years), voters elect a replacement at the next statewide primary (majority + runoff at general). If later, LG serves the remainder.
- Other statewide officers recalled: vacancy filled per existing rules → Governor appoints (through the end of... typically the appointee serves until the next election — actually for constitutional officers, appointees serve the remainder? For vacancies in statewide offices, the Governor appoints; for some offices the appointee serves until the next election... In California, an appointed AG/SoS etc. serves the remainder of the term? E.g., Alex Padilla appointed to replace Kamala Harris as Senator served until the next election, but that's US Senate. For state constitutional offices — when Xavier Becerra resigned as AG, Becerra was replaced by Rob Bonta who served the remainder of the term (then won election). Yes, appointees to constitutional offices serve the remainder.
- Legislators recalled: special election (existing vacancy rules), and the recalled legislator can run in it.

Now, the analysis. Let me weigh:

The strongest pro argument: the plurality-winner successor problem. This is real. In 2021, Larry Elder led replacement polls with ~38% in some polls but the field was 46; he could have won with a quarter of the vote in a state of 22 million voters, while Newsom had won 2018 by 62-38. That's genuinely undemocratic. Good government groups (LWV, Common Cause) back the reform. Most states with recalls don't have same-day successor elections.

The strongest con arguments:
(a) The measure's motivation: authored by Josh Newman (recalled in 2018 after the gas tax vote) and placed on the ballot by legislative Democrats after the 2021 Newsom recall. It looks like incumbent/Democratic establishment protection. The "Newman's Revenge" narrative. However, on the merits, motivation doesn't determine whether the policy is good.
(b) The provision allowing recalled officials to run in the replacement special election. Confirmed in the text: the current "The officer may not be a candidate" line is deleted, and only an appointment ban is added. This is a genuine, unforced flaw. Effects: a recalled legislator can run in the special election to fill their own seat — months later, low turnout, and they keep unlimited recall-defense funds? (The Chronicle points out incumbents facing recall can raise unlimited contributions; using that war chest in the special election is a big advantage.) So the recall becomes a temporary suspension rather than removal. This severely undermines the recall's accountability function for legislators. And for the governor case in the first-two-years scenario, could the recalled Governor run in the special election to replace themselves? The text of Art. V Sec 10(b) doesn't prohibit it; Art. II Sec 15(c) as amended only prohibits *appointment* of the recalled officer to the vacancy. So a recalled governor could run in the special election to succeed themselves! That is bizarre: e.g., a governor recalled in year 1 could run in the primary-months-later to get the office back. Combined with the LG serving in the interim, the recall's meaning is diluted.
(c) Governor-appointment power for other statewide offices — a partisan flip mechanism.
(d) Cost/vacancy for legislative seats.
(e) Popular opposition: PPIC 59-35 against.

Counter-considerations for a Yes: the LWV/Common Cause/Schnur argument — recall's original purpose is removal, not installing a successor via 25% plurality; alignment with vacancy rules; majority-rule protection; the gubernatorial early-term special election with majority + runoff is a clean majoritarian process.

Letting the recalled official run in the special election lets voters make the final call. One could argue this is *more* democratic (the special election is a normal election with normal campaign finance limits, unlike the recall replacement free-for-all... wait, is the special election subject to normal contribution limits? Yes, special elections have normal limits. The unlimited fundraising applies to committees "controlled by an officeholder who is the subject of a recall" — Gov. Code 85315. Could that money be used in the special election? The Chronicle says state law prohibits using recall-defense money for other campaigns, but a recalled official in a special election... "is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received." OK.)

So how do I weigh this? The question asks for a recommendation: yes or no.

Consider the decision-relevant factors:

1. Frequency: recalls are rare (11 on ballot since 1913, 6 successful). The measure's practical effect is small either way. But constitutional rules matter for the big event (gubernatorial recall).

2. The central question: who should fill a vacancy created by recall — the voters simultaneously (plurality), or via standard vacancy rules (succession/appointment/special election)?

Most democratic theorists would say: the recall's purpose is removal; the successor should be chosen by a process that ensures majority support. And Prop 5 deletes this sentence and replaces with vacancy + no-appointment rule.

So yes: under Prop 5, a recalled official may run in the subsequent special election (for legislative seats or the early-term gubernatorial special election). Confirmed.

Is that bad? Consider: Newman was recalled in 2018 over the gas tax, then re-elected in 2020 to the same seat. His case shows that the voters of his district, given a normal election, chose him back. Under current rules, he was barred from the 2018 successor race. Under Prop 5, he could have run in the special election months later — and if his constituents still wanted him (like 2020), they could have him back quickly, saving the 2020 re-election. Yes on 5:
- McClatchy California editorial board (Sacramento Bee, Fresno Bee, Modesto Bee, Merced Sun-Star, San Luis Obispo Tribune)

- Mark Barabak (LA Times columnist, personal — sympathetic)

No on 5:
- SF Chronicle editorial board
- Mercury News & East Bay Times editorial boards (BANG/SCNG: Santa Cruz Sentinel, SGV Tribune, LA Daily News, Press Enterprise)
- San Diego Union-Tribune editorial board
- Election Integrity Project California
- California Republican Party, legislative Republicans

No LA Times editorial board position found (as of Sept 30; maybe none at all).

Polling: PPIC Sept 2026: 59% no / 35% yes. Fundraising: essentially none on either side — a low-salience measure.

Now, the decision. Let me weigh the substance one more time, then commit.

Substance:

Genuine problem being addressed: In California's two-question recall, a replacement can take office with a small plurality (e.g., 2021 polls suggested Larry Elder ~mid-30s or less in a 46-candidate field; 2003 had 135 candidates). This can incentivize partisan "redo" recalls: the incumbent is removed by a narrow majority while the successor is installed with far less support. Also, the sitting officeholder can't run to succeed themselves, and an unlimited-fundraising loophole exists for recall targets. It's an outlier format among states.

The proposed remedy and its side effects:
1. Recall ballot = single yes/no question on removal. Good: simpler, focused.
2. Governor recalled → LG becomes Governor for the remainder; only if the recall happens in the first two years of the term before the next statewide primary's filing deadline does a replacement special election occur (majority required, top-two runoff). Concern: for recalls in the back half of a term, voters get no say at all in the successor — the LG (usually the same party/ticket) simply inherits. In 2021's scenario, had Newsom been recalled, Kounalakis would have served out the term. The will of the recall majority (they wanted change) would be nullified in governance terms. But note the recall itself is still meaningful (removing the individual).
3. Other statewide officers recalled → Governor appoints (serving the remainder). Concern: this can flip partisan control of an office via recall + appointment, arguably creating a new weaponization incentive for the governor's party. And it removes voters from the replacement decision.
4. Legislators recalled → seat vacant until special election (months, millions in costs, district unrepresented).
5. Recalled officials may run to fill their own vacancy (special elections) — the current constitutional ban on being a candidate is deleted; only appointment is barred. This is the most criticized feature: recall becomes a temporary suspension, and the recalled official (with recall-defense unlimited money and name ID) can win back the seat months later in a low-turnout special election, undoing the recall's effect. Even the author couldn't explain this provision ("I'm honestly not sure... It wouldn't pain me if it wasn't there").

Also, the fiscal effect is unknown/mixed; the state has had only 11 state-level recalls qualify since 1913 (6 successful), so the system isn't in crisis.

On the merits:
- The strongest argument for Yes: majority rule. The Chronicle itself concedes "we might support its removal in isolation." Good-gov groups (LWV, Common Cause) make the democracy argument: recalls shouldn't be vehicles to install 25% successors.
- The strongest arguments for No: (a) takes the voters' choice of replacement away (giving it to the LG, the Governor, or a delayed, more expensive special election); (b) the provision allowing recalled officials to run to replace themselves is an unforced, glaring error that undermines the recall entirely; (c) motivated by incumbent/political-establishment protection (Newman's Revenge); (d) the problem is rare; a cleaner reform could come later; (e) widespread editorial opposition across the spectrum; (f) voters oppose it 59-35 per PPIC.

Judgment: I think the balance tilts to NO. The core reform has merit, but the specific package on offer: (1) allows a just-recalled official to run in the election to replace themselves — meaning the recall could end with the same person back in office (with the fundraising advantages of incumbency), gutting the recall's accountability purpose; (2) hands replacement power for constitutional officers to gubernatorial appointment (partisan-flip risk) and for late-term governors to automatic succession with zero voter input; (3) leaves districts unrepresented for months and adds special-election costs; and (4) was transparently motivated by protecting incumbents after the 2018 gas-tax recall and the 2021 Newsom recall. California's current recall process, whatever its flaws, keeps the replacement decision with voters — which is the whole point of the recall power. And there's no urgency: 11 state recalls in 110+ years. Reject and wait for a cleaner fix.

I'll answer "no."

PROP
5
CHANGES RECALL ELECTION PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by the Legislature
Under current law, voters elect replacement candidates at the same time as the recall election. This measure instead fills recall vacancies by subsequent special election or appointment. Fiscal Impact: Net fiscal effect unknown. In the event of a recall, savings or costs of millions of dollars to administer the election depending on the office recalled. Supporters: None submitted Opponents: None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: Recall elections would no longer include a question about who should fill the vacancy. Instead, vacancies typically would be filled through special elections or appointments, depending on the office and timing.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: Voters would continue to be asked who should fill the vacancy as part of recall elections.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Proposition 5 restores the recall to its original purpose: removing corrupt officials. It closes the loophole that allows replacements to win with a small fraction of the vote, reducing the politics and costs of future recalls. Endorsed by League of Women Voters of California and California Common Cause. Vote YES
CON
Proposition 5 degrades California’s century-old recall process by limiting voters’ right to select a replacement for recalled officials. Instead, when statewide elected officials are recalled, other politicians would choose a replacement. For lower offices, another costly, taxpayer-funded election would come months later, leaving the office vacant and the people unrepresented.

PROP
5
CHANGES RECALL ELECTION PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
Election of State Officials. The State Constitution establishes legislative, executive, and judicial state offices. Some state officials represent parts of the state, known as districts. Other state officials, like the Governor or Attorney General, represent the entire state. Voters elect people to represent them in state offices for set terms. For example, a state Assembly Member is elected to a two-year term and the Governor is elected to a four-year term. To run for a state office, candidates must submit specific nomination documents before the election. State law sets when this “nomination period” occurs.
Recall of State Officials. The State Constitution allows voters to remove state officials from office before their term ends through a recall. A recall is an election in which voters are asked whether to remove an official from office. To qualify a recall for the ballot, supporters of the recall must collect a certain number of signatures from the official’s district (or statewide for statewide offices). Since 1913, 11 state recall efforts have qualified for the ballot (nine legislators and two Governors) and six have resulted in an official’s removal from office (five legislators and one Governor).
Two Questions in Recall Elections. In a recall election, voters are asked two questions: (1) whether the official should be removed from office and (2) who should replace the official if removed from office. The number of candidates appearing in the second question varies. For example, there were 135 candidates in the 2003 Governor recall election and 46 candidates in the 2021 Governor recall election. If a state official is recalled, the person who receives the most votes in the second question assumes the office.
Vacant State Offices. State officials may leave office before the end of their term for reasons other than a recall. For example, they may die or resign. When this happens, the office becomes vacant. The process to fill a vacant office varies by office. Typically, a vacant seat in the Assembly or Senate is filled through a special election called by the Governor. The Lieutenant Governor serves as Governor when there is a vacancy in the office of the Governor. Vacancies in other executive offices (for example, the Lieutenant Governor or Attorney General) and the Supreme Court and Courts of Appeal are filled by appointments by the Governor.
Frequency of Elections. Statewide elections in California are scheduled every two years. In scheduled election years, a primary election is held in either March or June, depending on the year, and a general election is held in November. In addition to scheduled elections, the state and local governments may call special elections to address specific issues. For example, the Governor may call a special election to fill a vacant Assembly seat.
Elections Administration in California. County elections officials administer most elections in California. As part of this work, they print and mail ballots and other voting materials to registered voters. Some state agencies also have election-related workload. For example, the Secretary of State oversees elections across the state and prepares and mails the state Voter Information Guide .
Paying for State Recall Elections. State law requires the California Department of Finance to work with state and local elections officials to estimate the cost of a recall election for a state office. The department is required to send the estimate to the Legislature. The Legislature reviews the estimate and may provide funding for the election. Any remaining costs are paid by the Secretary of State’s and counties’ budgets.
PROPOSAL
As described below, Proposition 5 changes the recall process to make it like the existing process for filling vacant state offices, except for the process to recall the Governor.
Removes Second Question From Recall Elections. Proposition 5 removes the second question—who should replace a recalled official—from a recall election. This means, in future recall elections, voters would only decide whether to remove an elected official from a state office, not who would replace the official.
Specifies Steps for Filling Vacant Offices. If a state official is recalled, Proposition 5 makes the office of the recalled official vacant. Except for the office of the Governor, Proposition 5 uses the existing process for filling vacancies to fill the office. In the case of an office in the state Senate or Assembly, this means that a replacement typically would be elected through a separate special election. The Governor would choose who would fill a vacancy in any other office (other than office of the Governor).
Creates Separate Process for Filling the Office of the Governor. The process for filling the office of the Governor depends on when the recall occurs. If the Governor is recalled before the close of the nomination period for the next statewide election during the first two years of the term, Proposition 5 says that the Lieutenant Governor serves as Governor until voters elect a new Governor at a future statewide election. If the Governor is recalled later in the term, the Lieutenant Governor serves as Governor for the rest of the term.
FISCAL EFFECTS
Fiscal Effects Depend on Frequency of Recalls and the Offices Recalled. Whether there would be costs or savings compared with today depends on the frequency of future recalls and the offices recalled. A recall of a statewide office (for example, Lieutenant Governor) would affect state elections officials and local elections officials in all 58 counties. A recall of a district-based office (for example, a state Senator or Assembly Member) would only affect state elections officials and local elections officials in those districts.
Potential Costs. Proposition 5 could result in higher costs associated with future recall elections if a special election is necessary to fill the vacant office after a recall. For example, a legislative office made vacant after a recall typically would be filled through a special election. If that special election could not be consolidated with a scheduled election, elections officials would need to run a standalone special election. The cost to state and local elections officials to administer such a special election could be millions of dollars per election.
Potential Savings. Proposition 5 could result in lower costs by removing the second question from the ballot. These savings would occur when a Governor is recalled in the latter part of the term and for other offices where vacancies are filled by appointment. There would be savings because ballots and voting materials would no longer include information about replacement candidates. The amount of savings would depend on how many candidates there would have been on the ballot if the second question remained but could be millions of dollars per election.
Net Effect Depends on Circumstances of Future Recall Efforts. The net fiscal effect is unknown because it depends on future recall elections. Proposition 5 could lead to savings or costs potentially in the range of millions of dollars to administer recall elections. How these savings or costs would be shared by state and county governments would depend on future decisions by the Legislature. This net fiscal effect represents less than one-tenth of 1 percent (0.1 percent) of the state’s total General Fund budget. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.)

PROP
5
CHANGES RECALL ELECTION PROCESS FOR STATEWIDE OFFICERS. LEGISLATIVE CONSTITUTIONAL AMENDMENT.
ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 5
California’s recall process should protect our democracy by allowing for the removal of an elected official who is corrupt or abusing their power. It should never be used as a tactic to ‘redo’ an election as a political or partisan scheme. Proposition 5 will restore the recall to its original purpose by making it fair, democratic, and accountable to the will of the majority.
Under current law, a statewide recall ballot asks voters two questions in sequence:
(1) Should the official be recalled? (2) If so, who should replace them?
By being connected, these two questions create a dangerous loophole. An elected official can be removed by a narrow majority. Then, a candidate listed in question #2 can win the office with far less than 50% of the votes cast in the election. This encourages political actors to target officials they couldn’t defeat in a regular election and to install replacements who lack broad public support.
We saw this play out in the 2021 gubernatorial recall. Voters rejected it decisively. The recall lost by nearly the same number of votes that the Governor won the regular election with. But California taxpayers were forced to spend more than $200 million on an election whose outcome simply reconfirmed what voters had already decided. Nearly 70% of California likely voters called the effort a waste of taxpayer money. And had the recall succeeded, the leading replacement candidate would have taken office with support from only about 28% of all recall voters.
Proposition 5 makes a single, commonsense change: it removes the second question from the recall ballot .
Under Prop. 5, in a state-level recall, voters would decide one very simple and important question: whether an officeholder should be removed. If a majority votes yes, that office becomes vacant and is filled under existing vacancy rules. If a Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor would become Governor and if the recall occurs early enough, voters would elect a replacement at the next statewide election; other statewide officers would be filled by appointment under existing rules; legislative seats by special election. No shortcuts, no loopholes, and no replacement candidate winning office without majority voter support.
In most states with recalls, vacancies are already filled by succession or a separate election, not a same-day replacement contest.
By eliminating the second question, Proposition 5 removes the incentive and ability to weaponize recalls as a shortcut for partisan advantage. Recalls could not be gamed to overturn the results of regular elections or install candidates who couldn’t win under normal conditions.
The framers of our recall process intended to safeguard voters against corrupt and unaccountable officials, not to provide a weapon for political operators to undo election results they don’t like. Proposition 5 preserves the recall as a tool for accountability while preventing it from being used to sidestep regular elections and majority rule.
Vote YES on Proposition 5 to protect majority rule, defend taxpayers, and restore California’s recall process back to the voters it was designed to serve.
Lorrel Plimier , Co-President
League of Women Voters of California
Darius L. Kemp , MPA, Executive Director
California Common Cause
Dan Schnur , Former Chair
California Fair Political Practices Commission
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT IN FAVOR OF PROPOSITION 5
Disregard the mental gymnastics the other side is doing here to tie us in knots and try to make sense of the truly nonsensical.
They say Proposition 5 “protects democracy.” It does the opposite-it erodes one of the fundamental elements of our recall process: to choose who replaces the recalled politician.
That’s not protecting democracy-that’s protecting political elites.
They call California’s system a “dangerous loophole.” It’s worked for 100 years, ousting politicians who abuse their office and replacing them with whoever the voters decide will do better.
Proposition 5 would create a loophole, not close one. The other side is gaslighting you. They think you won’t notice. Don’t be fooled.
If it ain’t broke, don’t fix it. Our recall process is only ‘broke’ for those who find themselves on the business end of it, like Proposition 5’s author did when he raised taxes after breaking campaign promises.
Now, he wants to burn it down on his way out the door-making future recalls less effective and keeping politicians like him less accountable.
If you traded in your car, would you want to know what you were getting in return-or would you be happy to sign it away and let the salesman stick you in a jalopy of their choosing after you’ve already committed? That’s what Proposition 5 asks you to do.
Our recall system will continue to work just fine, if we don’t let political elites with sour grapes tinker with it to their benefit.
Vote NO!
Brian W. Jones , Senate Minority Leader
Joe Patterson , Assemblymember
ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 5
Proposition 5 will take away your voice and erode your ability to remove and replace failed or corrupt politicians from office.
California politicians already have too much power. Proposition 5 gives them even more-and it does it by taking power away from you, the voters.
For over 100 years, California’s recall process has given us the ability to remove elected officials who abuse their office, break promises or fail to do the job they were elected to do. And, when that happens, the current process allows you-not politicians-to choose who replaces them.
Proposition 5 changes that system forever and takes power away from the people.
Today, a recall election asks two simple questions: Should the elected official be removed from office? If so, who should replace them? That means Californians can remove a failed politician and immediately choose someone new to take their place.
Proposition 5 keeps the first part but eliminates your ability to vote for a replacement.
Instead, Sacramento political insiders would decide what happens next. In many cases, politicians themselves-not voters-would choose who fills the vacancy, essentially allowing them to appoint another one of their friends or political allies to replace the one you just ousted.
In other cases, rather than an immediate replacement, the seat would sit vacant until another costly election-funded by you, the taxpayer-was scheduled months later. And here’s the kicker; that failed politician you just ran out the door for failure or corruption, they'd be allowed to run in that next election to regain control of the seat they just lost.
In either case, your vote matters less, and the political establishment gains more control.
Californians deserve the right to remove an elected official-and to choose who comes next. Proposition 5 takes away half of that right, and that’s wrong.
Supporters claim this measure improves democracy. It doesn’t. Democracy means voters-not Sacramento politicians-get to choose their leaders, when to give them the boot and who to replace them with. Proposition 5 undermines that fundamental concept.
Ask yourself: if you vote to remove a governor or another statewide elected official, shouldn’t you also decide who replaces them?
The answer is clear.
It’s also worth wondering why this measure is on the ballot in the first place. Why fix a system that isn’t broken and has been working just fine for over a century?
Well, the author of this proposal himself was recalled by California voters when he voted to raise gas taxes after promising not to. Instead of respecting the will of the people, he now wants to rewrite the rules and protect politicians like him from any meaningful accountability. California’s recall belongs to the people-not politicians. Protect your voice. Protect your vote. Protect your right to hold elected officials accountable.
Vote NO on Proposition 5.
Brian W. Jones , Senate Minority Leader
Joe Patterson , Assemblymember
REBUTTAL TO ARGUMENT AGAINST
PROPOSITION 5
Don’t be misled. Proposition 5 preserves your power to recall an official by majority vote while closing the loophole that allows a replacement candidate to take office with a small fraction of the vote.
Under current law, voters decide whether to remove an official by majority vote, but the replacement can win with far less than a majority. In 2021, a replacement candidate could have become Governor with support from 28% of recall voters. That is not majority rule.
Opponents want you to believe Proposition 5 takes away your right to choose. It does not. The real question is whether someone should become Governor with support from only a small fraction of California voters.
Proposition 5 preserves the recall while separating the decision to remove an officeholder from the decision about who should serve next. If a Governor is recalled, the Lieutenant Governor-elected statewide by California voters-provides continuity of government until voters choose the next Governor through a regular election. Voters will still choose their elected officials. But candidates seeking statewide office should earn that office in a regular election based on their qualifications, record, and plans for California, not use a recall as a shortcut to power.
A recall should decide whether an officeholder remains in office. Choosing who governs should happen in a regular election, where candidates earn the support of California voters. Proposition 5 protects the recall, respects majority rule, and ensures candidates run on their own merits. Vote YES on Proposition 5.
Lorrel Plimier , Co-President
League of Women Voters of California
Darius L. Kemp , MPA, Executive Director
California Common Cause

Endorsement: Prop 5 has a flaw so bizarre even its author doesn’t like it
Proposition 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
S.F. Chronicle from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Oct 8, 2026
So much has happened in American politics since 2021 that the recall election of California Gov. Gavin Newsom, which he overwhelmingly defeated, feels like a distant memory.
Proposition 5 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop5-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot puts recalls back in the spotlight.
Endorsement guide: S.F. Chronicle Endorsements for the 2026 California Election (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2026/california-sf-election-endorsements/)
Also: Y (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/supreme-court-judge-california-22431608.php)es or no? Here are the Chronicle’s endorsements for California Supreme Court and appeals courts (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/supreme-court-judge-california-22431608.php)
Authored by (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SCA1) former Democratic state Sen. Josh Newman of Fullerton — who was recalled in 2018, won reelection in 2020 and lost again in 2024 — Prop 5 would overhaul California’s process for recalling state-level officials.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Here’s how the current process works:
To recall a statewide official, proponents must gather signatures totaling at least 12% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the prior election. For the Newsom recall, that threshold was 1.3 million signatures (https://admin.cdn.sos.ca.gov/elections/ccrov/2025/march/25024ra.pdf). To recall members of the state Assembly and Senate, the minimum number of signatures is 20% of votes (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/recalls/recall-procedures-guide.pdf) cast for that office in the last election — for Newman’s recall, that threshold was about 63,600 signatures (https://www.sos.ca.gov/administration/news-releases-and-advisories/2018-news-releases-and-advisories/recall-signatures-senate-district-29-certified).
Once a recall qualifies, voters then receive a ballot with two questions — one, should this official be recalled, and two, who should replace them? — and a list of replacement candidates. If a simple majority votes in favor of the recall, the replacement candidate who receives the most votes wins — even if that candidate only gets a fraction of the votes against the recall.
The two-question setup is confusing — only six other states use it (https://www.ncsl.org/elections-and-campaigns/recall-of-state-officials). And permitting someone to be elected without majority support is undemocratic. Furthermore, given the distraction and price of recalls — Newsom’s cost about $200 million during (https://apnews.com/article/elections-california-legislature-gavin-newsom-state-legislature-f8b78745cc5376dc4836d914352f2116) the most fraught moments of the pandemic — they should be reserved for cases of serious misconduct or abject unfitness, not petty grievances.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Even though only 11 recalls of state-level officials have qualified for the ballot since 1913, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), California could benefit from raising the bar. Its signature-gathering threshold is among the lowest in the nation (https://lhc.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/Reports/266/Report266.pdf).
But Prop 5 doesn’t grapple with this issue.
Instead, it would eliminate the second question from the recall ballot, meaning voters would decide only whether the official should be removed.
If a majority says yes, one of three things would happen:
If the governor is recalled, the lieutenant governor would automatically step into the role. If the recall happens in the first half of a governor’s four-year term before the nomination period ends for the next statewide election, the lieutenant governor would serve until that election takes place and voters choose the next governor. But if the recall happens after that point, the lieutenant governor would finish the rest of the governor’s term.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
If another statewide official — such as the lieutenant governor, attorney general or secretary of state — is recalled, the governor would appoint their replacement. The governor already follows this process for statewide officials who die, resign or accept a different job.
And if a member of the state Legislature is recalled, the governor would call a special election for their replacement — mirroring the existing process for a lawmaker who dies, resigns or takes a different job. As the Legislative Analyst’s office notes (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop5-110326.pdf), if this special election couldn’t be consolidated with an already scheduled election, it could cost state and local election officials “millions of dollars” to administer.
Newman argued to us that eliminating the second question reduces “partisan games” and prevents candidates with minority support from winning elections.
We agree that the second question is problematic and we might support its removal in isolation. But Prop 5 contains a completely unnecessary provision that permits recalled officials to run in the very special election designed to replace them — overturning a ban in the California Constitution (https://law.justia.com/constitution/california/article-ii/section-15/).
This is particularly egregious because incumbents fighting recall attempts can generally raise unlimited funds from donors (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?sectionNum=85315.&lawCode=GOV). Although state law prohibits that money from being used for other campaigns, a recalled official in a special election is unlikely to forget whatever limitless support they received from wealthy special interests.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Newman himself couldn’t explain why Prop 5 contains that provision.
“I’m honestly not sure,” he said. “It wouldn’t pain me if it wasn’t there.”

But it is there. And the inability or unwillingness of lawmakers to put forth a simple, clean reform effort is reason enough for voters to reject this measure.
California’s recall process can certainly be improved, but the problem isn’t so dire that voters need to accept Prop 5’s glaring flaw.
